units.la: I. N. D. N. J. C.
units.tr: In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
DOMESTIC STUDIES: MEDITATIONS ON ETHICS AND POLITICS
PROFESSOR OF PHILOSOPHY IN THIS MOST FAMOUS

units.la: ACADEMIA PROFESS. ORD, AC P. T. PRO-RECTO-
units.tr: ACADEMY, ORDINARY PROFESSOR AND MAGNIFICENT PRO-RECTOR,
TO BE FOLLOWED WITH ALL RESPECTFUL OBSERVANCE BY HIS PUPIL,

units.la: Ad Diem 5. August. Anno M DC LXXI.
units.tr: On the 5th day of August, in the year 1671.
At the usual hour and place.

units.la: {E}Thica est prudentia, dirigens hominis actiones, ut, quantum in hac vita fieri potest, naturae viribus bene beateque vivat.
units.tr: Ethics is the prudence that directs human actions so that, as far as is possible in this life, a person lives well and happily by the powers of nature.

units.la: Hæc quamvis ex Ethnicorum Philosophorum libris deprompta, uti homini Christiano necessaria est; ita imprimis futurus JCtus eam prædiscere debet, juxta illud vulgatum: Ubi definit Ethicus, ibi incipit JCtus.
units.tr: Although this is drawn from the books of the heathen philosophers, it is necessary for a Christian man. So especially the future JCtus ought to learn it beforehand, according to the common saying: Where the ethicist ends, there the jurist begins.

units.la: Virtus, juxta Arist. est habitus animi, quo homo, bonus efficitur, ad munus suum bene & laudabiliter obeundum.
units.tr: Virtue, according to Aristotle, is a habit of the mind by which a man is made good, so that he discharges his office well and commendably.

units.la: Fortitudo est virtus moralis, servans mediocritatem circa metum & fiduciam.
units.tr: Courage is a moral virtue that keeps the mean with regard to fear and confidence.

units.la: Viri fortis est intrepidè adire, & constanter sustinere pericula, in quantum iis Reip prodesse, ac ita sibi gloriam conciliare potest: Hinc constat duello privato congredientes inter fortes non ponendos, nisi aliquando tale duellum publicâ nitatur authoritate. Nec illi in Virorum fortium Album collocandi, qui stipendii præcipuè causa, aut spe prædæ militant.
units.tr: It is the mark of a brave man to face dangers fearlessly and to endure them steadfastly, insofar as he can thereby serve the commonwealth and so win glory for himself. Hence it follows that those who fight a private duel are not to be counted among the brave, unless such a duel rests on public authority. Nor are those to be enrolled in the roll of brave men who fight chiefly for pay or in hope of plunder.

units.la: Vir fortis, fidem hosti semel datam nullo pacto violare potest.
units.tr: A brave man can in no way break a pledge once given to an enemy.

units.la: Temperantia est virtus, servans mediocritatem in expetendis & fruendis iis rebus, quæ gustum tactumve aliqua voluptate afficiunt. Dividitur in frugalitatem & castitatem; Illi in excessu opponitur Voracitas & Ebrietas. Huic libido & impudicitia.
units.tr: Temperance is a virtue that keeps the mean in desiring and enjoying those things which affect taste and touch with some pleasure. It is divided into frugality and chastity. Opposed to the excess of the former are gluttony and drunkenness; to the latter, lust and impurity.

units.la: Ebrietatem esse majus vitium libidine demonstrabimus, tàm ex principiis naturalibus, quàm Ethicis (Nota) ultraque non vagabimur.
units.tr: We will demonstrate that drunkenness is a greater vice than lust, both from natural principles and from ethical ones (Note), and we shall not wander beyond either.

units.la: Veneris affectus utut vehementissimus & impetuosissimus sit, ( quod etiam fatetur Imperator in N. 74. c. 4. pr. Furore amoris nihil vehementius est, quem retinere Philosophia est perfecta :) remedia tamen ad hunc refrænandum præsto sunt :
units.tr: However vehement and impetuous the passion of love may be (which the Emperor also admits in N. 74, c. 4 pr.: Nothing is more vehement than the fury of love, which it is the mark of perfect philosophy to restrain), remedies to curb it are nonetheless at hand:

units.la: Ethici quatuor potissimùm numerant : Otii fugam, Occasionis evitationem, victûs moderationem, assiduam ad Deum precationem.
units.tr: The ethicists chiefly enumerate four: flight from idleness, avoidance of occasion, moderation of diet, and constant prayer to God.

units.la: Vitæ humanæ terminum fatalem esse concedimus, interim tamen eum temperantiâ prolongari posse, non negamus.
units.tr: We concede that the term of human life is fated, yet we do not deny that it can be lengthened by temperance.

units.la: Liberalitati opponuntur prodigalitas & avaritia. Avaritia tamen prodigalitate multò deterior est. Prodigus enim facilè sanari potest, aut ætatis maturitate, aut inopiâ ; At avaritia senio augetur, simul & inopiâ. Et prodigus multis prodest, avarus verò nec sibi nec aliis quicquam prodest, sed nocet ubi & quâcunque ratione potest.
units.tr: Prodigality and avarice are opposed to liberality. Yet avarice is far worse than prodigality. For the prodigal can easily be cured, either by coming of age or by poverty; but avarice grows with old age, and with poverty as well. And the prodigal does good to many, whereas the avaricious man does no good either to himself or to others, but harms them wherever and however he can.

units.la: Magnanimitas est virtus, mediocritatem in magnis & debitis honoribus expetendis servans.
units.tr: Magnanimity is a virtue that keeps the mean in seeking great and due honours.

units.la: Magnanimi itaq; fundamentum, quo, studio magnorum honorum, nititur, est ipsa virtus.
units.tr: The foundation on which the magnanimous man rests in his pursuit of great honours is virtue itself.

units.la: Magnanimus Vir optimus est, habetque in unaquaque Virtute magnum aliquid atque excellens, ipsaque magnanimitas virtutum quoddam ornamentum est.
units.tr: The magnanimous man is an excellent man, and in every virtue he has something great and outstanding; magnanimity itself is a certain adornment of the virtues.

units.la: Magnanimus ergo non ambit, nisi magnos honores, & a bonis ac claris tantum viris deferri solitos; idque non nimis cupide aut sollicite, ne rem novam sibi ac insolitam, sed ut mercedem Virtutis sibi debitam, petere, videri possit. Magnanimus non in honore tantum, sed etiam in divitiis & omni fortuna moderatum sese praebet, neque in secundis rebus effertur laetitia, neque in adversis superatur moerore.
units.tr: The magnanimous man therefore seeks only great honours, such as are customarily bestowed only upon good and distinguished men; and he seeks them not too eagerly or anxiously, lest he appear to be seeking something new and unusual, but as a reward for virtue that is rightfully his. The magnanimous man shows himself moderate not only in honour but also in wealth and in every kind of fortune: he is not elated with joy in prosperity, nor overcome with grief in adversity.

units.la: Magnanimus neminem metuit, hinc fit, ut aperte se vel inimicum vel amicum profiteatur, utque Veritatem potius curet, quam opinionem, omnia, quae agat & dicat aperte, nihil dissimulet. Ex quo sequitur nihil difficilius Magnanimo esse, quàm alterius nutu atque arbitratu vivere: Est enim hoc servile. Arist. 4. c. 3.
units.tr: The magnanimous man fears no one. Hence it follows that he openly declares himself either an enemy or a friend, and that he cares more for the truth than for opinion, concealing nothing of what he does or says openly. From this it follows that nothing is more difficult for the magnanimous man than to live at another's nod and will, for this is servile. Arist. 4. c. 3.

units.la: Beneficia libenter non dat nisi cum verecundia: Illud enim praestantioris hoc inferioris hominis est; Si quae tamen accipit, ea statim majori mensura compensat, & bene de se meritum novo beneficio devincit. Hinc fit ut datorum citius, quàm acceptorum beneficiorum memoriam deponat, libentiusque audiat commemorare, quos ipse beneficiis affecit, quàm à quibus beneficiis affectus est. Porrò magnanimus se aliis prudenter accommodat: inter magnos & graves, magnum se ac gravem praebet, inter mediocres & humiles gravitatem comitate temperat. Generosum enim est, inter magnos gravitatem praese ferre, inter humiles ridiculum est. Arist. d. c. 2.
units.tr: He bestows benefits willingly, but only with modesty, for that belongs to the superior man, whereas to receive is the mark of the inferior. Yet if he does accept something, he repays it at once with a greater measure, and binds the one who has deserved well of him to himself by a new benefit. Hence he forgets the benefits he has bestowed more quickly than those he has received, and he more gladly hears those recounted whom he has himself benefited than those by whom he has been benefited. Moreover, the magnanimous man adapts himself prudently to others: among the great and serious he shows himself great and serious, while among the middling and humble he tempers his gravity with courtesy. For it is noble to display gravity among the great, but ridiculous among the humble. Arist. d. c. 2.

units.la: Utrum magnanimus injurias recordari atque ulcisci debeat?
units.tr: Whether the magnanimous man ought to remember injuries and take revenge for them?

units.la: Commendatur Philippus, Macedonum Rex, quòd omnes suos conviciatores, Patientiâ tiâ vicerit, eosque clementiâ & placabilitate suâ ex inimicis, amicos sibi reddiderit. Nemo, inquit Titus apud Xiphilinum, me injuriâ afficere, vel contumeliâ insequi potest; Propterea, quòd nihil ago, quod reprehendi mereatur, ea verò, quæ falsa de me dicuntur, prorsus negligo; Quem alleg. Gothofr. ad l. unic. C. si quis Imper. Maled. Nobis placet distinguere inter injurias graves seu famosas & cavillationes seu obtrectationes.
units.tr: Philip, King of Macedon, is commended because he overcame all his revilers by his patience, and by his clemency and readiness to forgive turned them from enemies into friends. "No one," says Titus in Xiphilinus, "can wrong me or pursue me with insults, because I do nothing that deserves reproach, and I altogether disregard what is said falsely about me." Cited by Gothofredus on l. unic. C. si quis Imper. Maled. We think it right to distinguish between grave or defamatory injuries and taunts or disparagements.

units.la: CUm homo omnium animalium dignissimum sit ac præstantissimum, cujus gratia rerum natura omnia comparavit. Teste Cajo in l. 28. §. 1. de usur.
units.tr: Since man is the most worthy and excellent of all animals, the sake of whom nature arranged all things. So Gaius, in l. 28 §1 de usur.

units.la: Nemini non obvium esse potest, quàm Nobilis, quàmque pretiosa sit Politices disciplina, eòque perpendenda & discenda accuratiùs, quia nullum animal, homine, est morosius, quodque majori cura & arte tractandum dum sit, monente Seneca lib.1. de elem. cap.17. Prudenti igitur consilio non impetu hic opus est. Curt. Et omnes qui magnarum rerum consilia suscipiunt, æstimare debent, an quod inchoatur Reip. utile ipsiq; gloriosum sit. Tacit.
units.tr: Nothing is more obvious to anyone than how noble and how valuable the discipline of politics is, and therefore it must be weighed and learned more carefully, since no animal is more troublesome than man, and none needs to be handled with greater care and skill, as Seneca warns in Book 1 of De elementis, ch. 17. Prudent counsel, therefore, not impulse, is needed here. Curt. And all who undertake the counsels of great affairs ought to consider whether what is begun is useful to the commonwealth and glorious for themselves. Tacit.

units.la: Utrum autem in Prisco innocentiæ statu, si primi hominum parentes lapsi non fuissent, Politicâ societate & disciplina opus fuisset? Plurimi id negant nos affirmativè defendemus.
units.tr: But whether, in the original state of innocence, political society and discipline would have been necessary had our first parents not fallen? Most deny it; we will defend the affirmative.

units.la: Definitur Politica, quod sit prudentia, rempubl. rectè constituendi ac gubernandi. Qui itaque reipubl. rectè constituendæ, administrandæ, corrigendæ & conservandæ prudentiâ instructus est, proprie Politicus dicitur.
units.tr: Politics is defined as the prudence of rightly constituting and governing a commonwealth. Therefore whoever is instructed in the prudence of rightly constituting, administering, correcting and preserving a commonwealth is properly called a Politicus.

units.la: Quamvis improprie hoc nomen quoque sibi arrogent suaves quidem & elegantes homines, qui moribus decoris & amabilibus in sermone & gestu utuntur, & hominum animos blandis & plerumque fucatis verbis sibi conciliare, & in commodum suum trahere affabrè norunt. Quos Terent. in Andr. & post eum Waremund ab Ehrenberg in tr. de foederibus vivis coloribus depingunt.
units.tr: Yet improperly this name is also claimed by smooth and elegant men, who use decorous and pleasing manners in speech and gesture, know skilfully how to win men's minds with flattering and mostly feigned words, and how to draw them to their own advantage. Terence in the Andria, and after him Waremund ab Ehrenberg in his treatise on living covenants, paint these men in vivid colours.

units.la: Qui homines licet gerendis rebus magis sint idonei, quàm agrestes & morosæ conversationis: Ethici tamen magis seu Politi, quàm Politici audire debent.
units.tr: Such men, although they are more fit for managing affairs than rustic and surly company, ought nevertheless to be heard as Ethicists or Politi rather than as Politici.

units.la: Improprie insuper Politici vocantur, callidi veteratores & Machiavelli sectarii, qui fronte quidem Politi apparent, sed astutam vapido servant sub pectore Vulpem, quique in omni vita scenæ & foro belle servientes, ex ancipiti temporum mutatione pendent, perque fas & nefas privatum suum commodum quærunt, quibus Auth. des Alamodischen Politici.
units.tr: Improperly, too, are called Politici the crafty old hands and followers of Machiavelli, who indeed appear at the front as Politi, but keep a sly fox under a tepid breast, who, serving well in every part of life, on the stage and in the forum, hang upon the uncertain changes of the times and seek their private advantage by right and wrong; to whom the Author of Des Alamodischen Politici applies the name.

units.la: Politia sive politica societas originem à natura trahit, quam naturæ propensionem excitaverunt, tum egestas, tum periculum.
units.tr: Politia, or civil society, takes its origin from nature; this natural inclination was roused both by want and by danger.

units.la: Respublica est societas plurium familiarum sub eodem magistratu, iisdemque legibus degentium.
units.tr: A commonwealth is a society of several families living under the same magistrate and the same laws.

units.la: Reipublicæ formas seu species statuimus tres & quidem simplices, mixtas haud agnoscimus. Committitur enim summum imperium vel uni homini, vel concilio sive curiæ uni multorum hominum.
units.tr: We lay down three forms or kinds of commonwealth, all of them simple; we do not recognise mixed ones. For supreme power is entrusted either to a single man, or to a council or senate of many men.

units.la: Rursus concilium multorum hominum, vel est omnium civium ita, ut quilibet eorum jus habeat suffragii, possitque interesse rebus discutiendis, si voluerit; vel partis tantum est. Unde hæ tres nascuntur civitatis species. Una ubi summum imperium est penes concilium, in quo quilibet civis jus habet suffragii, & vocatur Democratia. Altera ubi summum imperium penes concilium, in quo non omnes, sed certa aliqua pars suffragium habet, & dicitur Aristocratia. Tertia ubi summum imperium penes unum est, & appellatur Monarchia. In primâ, is, qui rerum potitur, Populus. In secundâ, Optimates. In tertiâ, Monarcha nominatur.
units.tr: Again, a council of many men is either that of all the citizens, so that each of them has a right to vote and may attend the discussion of affairs if he wishes, or it belongs to only a part. Hence arise these three kinds of state. In the first, where supreme power lies with a council in which every citizen has a right to vote, it is called Democracy. In the second, where supreme power lies with a council in which not all, but some certain part, has the vote, it is called Aristocracy. In the third, where supreme power lies with one man, it is called Monarchy. In the first, the one who holds the reins of affairs is the People. In the second, the Optimates. In the third, he is called the Monarch.

units.la: Hanc tanquam statum simplicissimum, antiquissimum, justissimum, & natura suâ firmissimum, atque ita mutationibus minimè obnoxium caeteris longæ præferimus, juxta illud Homeri : Iliad. 3.
units.tr: We prefer this state to the others, as the simplest, most ancient, most just, and by its nature most firm, and therefore least liable to change, following that saying of Homer: Iliad 3.

units.la: Haud bonum multorum dominatio, unus dominus esto Unus Rex, cui dedit Saturni filius, callidi ingenii Sceptrum atque jura, ut his regnet. Noxia rei plures Domini : Rex unicus esto. Multos imperitare malum est : Rex unicus esto. Non bene turba regit populum : Rex unicus esto.
units.tr: Rule of many is not good: let there be one lord, one king, to whom the son of crafty Saturn gave the sceptre and laws, that he might reign over them. Many masters are a harmful thing: let there be one king. To be commanded by many is an evil: let there be one king. A crowd does not rule a people well: let there be one king.

units.la: Jubet quidem natura, Imperium illud Monarchicum seu Principatum, Mari potius quàm fœminæ deferendum: Interim tamen hæ non penitus sunt removendæ, quia natura sæpè fœminas solertes facit, industria literatas, educatio probas ac pias, & experientia prudentes.
units.tr: Nature indeed directs that the monarchical rule, or principate, should pass to a male rather than a female; yet women are not therefore to be wholly shut out, since nature often makes women clever, learning makes them literate, upbringing makes them upright and pious, and experience makes them prudent.

units.la: Principatus legitimè acquiritur, Successione vel Electione, hæc est cùm spreto natalium jure, Princeps suffragiis designatur. Illa cùm gentilis is honos est, & Princeps è Principe nascitur. Electio quidem antiquior, successio tamen receptior, & adspectu aliquo melior: Quia verum est, minori discrimine summum Principem quàm quaeri. Tacit. vid. Lips. 2. Polit. 4. Mores tamen Regionum, pro natura & diversitate climatum hic attendendi.
units.tr: A principality is lawfully acquired by succession or by election. Election is when the prince is designated by votes, with the right of birth set aside. Succession is when the honour is hereditary and a prince is born of a prince. Election is the older practice, but succession is more common and in some respects better, because a supreme prince is found with less danger than he is sought, as Tacitus says; see Lipsius, Politics, book 2, chapter 4. Still, the customs of each region must be considered here, according to its nature and the diversity of climates.

units.la: Imperatori nostro Romano-Germ. iuste competere praecedentiam & praecellentiam prae omnibus aliis Regibus & Principibus, uti nemini (nisi unico Bodino. lib. 1. cap. 9. de Rep. dum somniat, Regis sui legatorum inscitia, Imperatores nostros hanc praerogativam adeptos:) hactenus dubium fuit, ita evidentissimis id rationibus demonstrari potest.
units.tr: That our Roman-German Emperor rightly holds precedence and pre-eminence over all other kings and princes, which no one has disputed until now except the lone Bodin (Republic, book 1, chapter 9), who dreams, through the ignorance of his own king's envoys, that our Emperors obtained this prerogative, can be demonstrated by the most evident reasons.

units.la: Ipse Turcarum Rex id agnoscit, & facto & stylo satis approbat, dum eidem ita scribit: <bl>Auß dem Potentaten Jesu dem vornehmsten / und zwischen dem Geschlechte Jesu erwehlten / fürnehmsten Herren aller Christlichen Völcker.</bl>
units.tr: The Turkish king himself acknowledges this, and by his deeds and his style sufficiently approves it, when he writes to him thus: "From the Potentate Jesus, the most eminent and chosen of the line of Jesus, the foremost Lord of all Christian peoples."

units.la: Accedit quòd aliorum Regum legatos, primum iis attribuendo locum, stantes, Imperatoris nostri vero sedentes audiat. Cumque Caroli V. Legatus coram Turcarum Rege aliquandiu stetisset, neque secundum morem consiconfidere jussus esset, pallio suo substrato insedit, ac ita mandata sui domini exposuit, finitaque oratione id in palatio reliquit, monitus vero, ut pallium secum sumeret, falsè respondit: Caesaris legatum sellam portare non solere. Vid. Arum. de jur. pub. disc. 1. pag. 9.
units.tr: Moreover, he gives the envoys of other kings a place of honour and hears them standing, but he hears those of our Emperor sitting. When the envoy of Charles V had stood for some time before the Turkish king, and had not been ordered to sit according to custom, he sat down on his cloak spread on the floor and set out his master's commands. When the speech was finished he left the cloak in the palace, and when he was reminded to take it with him he falsely replied: the envoy of Caesar is not accustomed to carry a seat. See Arumaeus, On Public Law, discourse 1, page 9.

units.la: An verò in hunc usque diem Imperat. nostri legati, illam praerogativam, quod sedentes mandata exponant, continuarint vid. Reinck. de Reg. sec. 1. classf. 2. c. 7. n. 51. 52. & 53. Refert Herm. fasc 1. publ. c. 4. n. 1.
units.tr: Whether our Emperor's envoys have continued to this day to keep that prerogative, of delivering their commissions while seated, see Reinkingk, On the Secular and Ecclesiastical Rule, book 1, class 2, chapter 7, numbers 51, 52 and 53. Hermann, Public Fasc. 1, chapter 4, number 1, also reports it.

units.la: Nostra memoria Anno 1634. in nuptiis designati Regis Daniae Christiani V. omnium fere ex Europa Principum legatis decoratis, novo, sed occulto ausu, ex humanitate, quam hospites hospitibus debent, praecedentiae fundamenta jaciendo, legatum Gallicum callidum suscepisse consilium sub officii enim & Curialitatis Aulicae specie, celsissimum Holsatiae Principem Fridericum, Ferdin. II. Imp. legatum in conclavi suo se invisere velle nunciavit, seque in congressu & discursu celsitudinis titulum Principi tributurum, modo sciret, tum dexterum sibi locum durante visitatione tributum , tùm excellentiæ titulo honoratum iri : quas machinationes Cæsareus legatus advertens , respondit : se nil mirari , si vel ab alio vel gallico legato celsissimi titulo honoraretur, sed injuriam fore non levem, si id non fieret , deinde se sponte nosse, quid loci , titulive hospiti tribuendum , & quam personam sustineret , proinde, uti penes legatum Gallicum esset , visitationem vel perficere, vel omittere ita & sibi omnino certum esse , nihil omittere aut facere , quod in ejusmodi solennitatibus , Majestati Imp. tantillum detrahere possit.
units.tr: In our own memory, in the year 1634, at the betrothal of the designated King of Denmark, Christian V, the envoys of nearly all the princes of Europe were present. The French envoy, with a new but hidden daring, and under the pretext of hospitality, which guests owe to guests, and of laying the foundations of precedence, devised a crafty plan. Under the guise of courtesy and court ceremony, he announced that he wished to visit the most high Prince Frederick of Holstein, the envoy of Emperor Ferdinand II, in his own chamber, and that in their meeting and conversation he would give the Prince the title of Highness, provided he knew that a place on his right would be given to him during the visit and that he would be honoured with the title of Excellency. The Imperial envoy, noticing these schemes, replied that he would not be surprised if he were given the title of Highness by another envoy or by the French envoy, but that it would be no slight injury if it were not done. He added that he himself knew well what place and title were to be given to a guest, and what person he represented. Therefore, it was for the French envoy to either make the visit or omit it. He was quite certain, he said, that he would neither omit nor do anything in such ceremonies that could take away even the slightest bit from the Majesty of the Emperor.
It is enough to have touched on these preliminaries for this time.

units.la: UNI & TRIUNO sit Gloria , in sempiterna Secula.
units.tr: To the One and Triune God be glory for ever and ever.

units.la: VNIVS TRIVNO In Gloria, in Lamentationis Scala.
units.tr: VNIVS TRIVNO In Gloria, in Lamentationis Scala.
